The same happens with quantities that are correlated, such as the slope and the intercept of one fit: the operators treat them as independent, so the uncertainty of a combination of both can be off.

docs.title: Numbers with an uncertainty¶
docs.text: A Parameter has a value, a unit, an uncertainty and bounds. Here is a length of 2 m with an uncertainty of 0.2 m, which a fit may vary between 0 and 10 m. The uncertainty is given as a variance, so it is written as the square of the error, $0.2^2 = 0.04\ \text{m}^2$:

docs.title: Error and uncertainty¶
docs.text:
In everyday language the two words are used for the same thing, and so does EasyScience: the property that holds the square root of the variance is called error. Strictly speaking they are not the same.

  • The error of a measurement is the difference between the measured value and the true value. The true value is usually unknown, so the error of a real measurement can seldom be stated.
  • The uncertainty is a quantitative estimate of the range around the measured value in which the true value is expected to lie. It describes the precision, or the doubt, of the measurement.

What EasyScience stores is an uncertainty, as a variance, and error is the standard uncertainty: one standard deviation. The standard deviation is a complete summary of the uncertainty only when the distribution of the values is symmetric and close to Gaussian. Then $\pm 1\sigma$ covers about 68 % of the possible values, and "error" and "uncertainty" can be used loosely. This is not always the case: for a skewed or heavy-tailed distribution, for a systematic effect that no repeated measurement reveals, or for a result that has gone through a strongly non-linear function, the same $\pm$ number can be misleading. What the word means depends on the context.

docs.title: Addition and subtraction¶
docs.text:
The operators work between Parameters, DescriptorNumbers and plain numbers. The result is a Parameter (with bounds) if any operand is a Parameter, and a DescriptorNumber otherwise.

Only numbers with the same physical dimension can be added. If the units differ, the second operand is converted to the unit of the first, so the result is in metres here:

docs.title: Uncertainty in a chart¶
docs.text: The uncertainty of a result depends on the inputs. A speed $v = d/t$ of an object that covered $3.0 \pm 0.1$ m is much less certain for short times than for long ones, even though the time has the same uncertainty of 0.05 s each time. The chart is interactive: hover over the curve to read the values. It loads Plotly from the internet, so it needs a connection. The charts are shown with a small helper, show_figure(fig), which is defined in a hidden cell; in your own notebook fig.show() does the same.

docs.title: Good to know¶
docs.text: An operator knows nothing about where its operands come from. The same object on both sides of an operator gives the right variance: $x - x$ is exactly $0 \pm 0$. But an intermediate result is a new, independent number: in $(2x)/x$ the $x$ cancels and the exact answer is $2 \pm 0$, yet 2 * x no longer remembers that it came from x. Bounds are combined in the same way, as if the operands were independent, so $x - x$ of a Parameter that may vary between 0 and 10 has bounds $[-10, 10]$:

docs.title: Correlation
docs.text:
Two measurements are correlated when their uncertainties are not independent: when one reading is too high (it deviates upwards from the true value), the other tends to be too high as well (positive correlation) or too low (negative correlation). This happens whenever the measurements share something, such as

  • the same instrument with the same, uncertain calibration, so that every reading is shifted or scaled in the same way,
  • the same zero point or reference,
  • two parameters of one fit, which compensate each other.

The strength of a correlation is the correlation coefficient $\rho = \text{cov}(x, y) / (\sigma_x \sigma_y)$, where $\sigma_x$ and $\sigma_y$ are the standard uncertainties of $x$ and $y$, the numbers after the $\pm$. It is a number between $-1$ and $+1$. For $\rho = 0$ the measurements are independent. With correlations the first-order propagation becomes

$$ \sigma_f^2 = \sum_i \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}\right)^2 \sigma_i^2 + 2 \sum_{i < j} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_j}\, \rho_{ij}\, \sigma_i \sigma_j . $$

For a sum $x + y$ this is $\sigma^2 = \sigma_x^2 + \sigma_y^2 + 2\rho\,\sigma_x\sigma_y$ and for a difference $x - y$ it is $\sigma^2 = \sigma_x^2 + \sigma_y^2 - 2\rho\,\sigma_x\sigma_y$.

A Parameter stores a variance and no covariance, so EasyScience always takes $\rho = 0$. This notebook shows what that costs and how to do better where it matters.

The function show(label, number) prints a number as value ± uncertainty unit and, for a Parameter with finite bounds, the bounds. The uncertainty is the attribute error; see the note in the arithmetic notebook.

In [2]: Copied! 
def show(label, number):
    """Print a labelled number as value ± uncertainty with its unit and, for a Parameter, bounds."""
    text = f'{label} = {number.value:.4f} ± {number.error or 0.0:.4f} {number.unit}'
    if hasattr(number, 'min') and (np.isfinite(number.min) or np.isfinite(number.max)):
        text += f'   in [{number.min + 0.0:.4f}, {number.max + 0.0:.4f}]'
    print(text)
def show(label, number): """Print a labelled number as value ± uncertainty with its unit and, for a Parameter, bounds.""" text = f'{label} = {number.value:.4f} ± {number.error or 0.0:.4f} {number.unit}' if hasattr(number, 'min') and (np.isfinite(number.min) or np.isfinite(number.max)): text += f' in [{number.min + 0.0:.4f}, {number.max + 0.0:.4f}]' print(text) In [4]: Copied! 
def gradient(func, values):
    """Derivatives of func with respect to each value, by central differences."""
    values = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)
    slopes = np.empty_like(values)
    for i, value in enumerate(values):
        step = 1e-6 * max(abs(value), 1.0)
        upper, lower = values.copy(), values.copy()
        upper[i] += step
        lower[i] -= step
        slopes[i] = (func(*upper) - func(*lower)) / (2 * step)
    return slopes


def propagate(func, values, sigmas, correlation=None):
    """First-order propagation: the value of func and its uncertainty."""
    sigmas = np.asarray(sigmas, dtype=float)
    if correlation is None:
        correlation = np.eye(len(sigmas))
    covariance = np.asarray(correlation, dtype=float) * np.outer(sigmas, sigmas)
    slopes = gradient(func, values)
    return func(*values), float(np.sqrt(slopes @ covariance @ slopes))


def report(label, result, unit):
    """Print a labelled (value, uncertainty) pair like show does."""
    print(f'{label} = {result[0]:.4f} ± {result[1]:.4f} {unit}')

docs.title: A helper that knows about correlation¶
docs.text: To propagate correlated uncertainties this notebook uses the helpers gradient and propagate. They work out the derivatives numerically and combine them with the formula above. propagate takes the function, the values, the standard uncertainties and, optionally, the matrix of correlation coefficients. Without it the inputs are independent. report prints a result like show does.

docs.title: The same ruler twice¶
docs.text: Two boards are measured one after the other with the same ruler: the first is 1.20 m long and the second 0.80 m. Each reading has a standard uncertainty of ±0.02 m. How strongly the two uncertainties are correlated depends on how much of them comes from the ruler that the readings share, for example an uncertain zero point: if the ruler reads a little long for one board, it does so for the other as well. If all of the uncertainty is shared, $\rho = +1$. First EasyScience's arithmetic, which takes $\rho = 0$, then the helper for different correlations:

docs.title: Exercise 1: Two sections, one ruler¶
docs.text: A rod is made of two sections measured with the same tape: 1.20 ± 0.02 m and 0.80 ± 0.03 m. Their uncertainties are strongly correlated, $\rho = 0.9$. What is the total length, with its uncertainty? Compare it with the uncertainty that EasyScience gives.

docs.title: Shared offsets cancel¶
docs.text: The most useful consequence of a positive correlation is in differences: an offset that both readings share drops out. A surveyor measures the heights of two points from the same station. The station height is uncertain, which shifts both readings in the same way. The uncertainty of their difference is much smaller than that of either height.

docs.title: Exercise 2: A height difference¶
docs.text: The heights of two points above a common station are 5.42 ± 0.05 m and 3.18 ± 0.05 m, with a correlation of $\rho = 0.95$ because of the shared station. What is the height difference, with its uncertainty? What does EasyScience report?

docs.title: Ratios of readings from one instrument¶
docs.text: If two intensities are read with the same detector, an uncertain gain makes both too large or both too small by the same fraction. In a ratio that factor cancels, again because the correlation is positive and the derivatives have opposite signs.

docs.title: Exercise 3: An intensity ratio¶
docs.text: Two intensities, 120.0 ± 6.0 and 80.0 ± 4.0 counts per second, were read with the same detector and are correlated with $\rho = 0.9$. What is their ratio $I_1 / I_2$, with its uncertainty? Compare it with the result of EasyScience.

docs.title: Correlation from a fit¶
docs.text: The best-known source of correlated numbers is a fit. The slope and the intercept of a straight line, $y = a x + b$, are strongly correlated whenever the $x$ values are far from zero: a steeper line must start lower to pass through the same data. A fit program reports their covariance matrix, and np.polyfit can return it too. These ten points lie close to a line:

docs.title: Exercise 4: Predicting from a fit¶
docs.text: A fit gave a slope of 0.50 ± 0.02 and an intercept of 2.0 ± 0.3, with a correlation of $-0.97$. What is the predicted $y$ at $x = 18$, with its uncertainty? What is the uncertainty if the correlation is ignored?

docs.title: Good to know¶
docs.text:
• A correlation coefficient has to come from somewhere: the covariance matrix of a fit, a calibration, or an argument about what the measurements share. It cannot be guessed from the values.
  • When the correlation is unknown, $\rho = +1$ and $\rho = -1$ give the largest and the smallest uncertainty that a combination can have, so they bracket the answer.
  • Correlated quantities often hide inside one analysis. If a result is built from several numbers that came from the same fit or the same instrument, ask whether the independence assumption of EasyScience holds.
  • A Parameter stores a value and a variance and nothing else, so there is no place for the covariance of two Parameters. Even numbers that came from the same fit, such as the slope and the intercept above, are treated as independent by EasyScience's arithmetic and by the functions of es.math. Until that changes, use a helper like propagate with the covariance matrix of the fit.

docs.title: Error propagation
docs.text:
A calculated result is only as certain as the measurements it is calculated from. Working out how the uncertainties of the measurements carry over to the result is usually called error propagation. As the note in the arithmetic notebook explains, the number it produces is an uncertainty (a statement about how well a value is known), so that is the word used here.

The result of a calculation depends on the measurements and on the formula that combines them. The same quantity can often be worked out in several ways, and the ways differ in how well they use the measurements. This notebook uses one example throughout: the area of a table top.

For independent inputs the uncertainty of $f(x_1, x_2, \dots)$ follows, to first order, from

$$ \sigma_f^2 = \sum_i \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}\right)^2 \sigma_i^2 . $$

The term $\partial f / \partial x_i \cdot \sigma_i$ is the contribution of measurement $i$: its uncertainty, scaled by how strongly the result reacts to it. A formula that reacts weakly to uncertain measurements gives a small uncertainty.

def gradient(func, values):
    """Derivatives of func with respect to each value, by central differences."""
    values = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)
    slopes = np.empty_like(values)
    for i, value in enumerate(values):
        step = 1e-6 * max(abs(value), 1.0)
        upper, lower = values.copy(), values.copy()
        upper[i] += step
        lower[i] -= step
        slopes[i] = (func(*upper) - func(*lower)) / (2 * step)
    return slopes


def propagate(func, values, sigmas, correlation=None):
    """First-order propagation: the value of func and its uncertainty."""
    sigmas = np.asarray(sigmas, dtype=float)
    if correlation is None:
        correlation = np.eye(len(sigmas))
    covariance = np.asarray(correlation, dtype=float) * np.outer(sigmas, sigmas)
    slopes = gradient(func, values)
    return func(*values), float(np.sqrt(slopes @ covariance @ slopes))


def report(label, result, unit):
    """Print a labelled (value, uncertainty) pair like show does."""
    print(f'{label} = {result[0]:.4f} ± {result[1]:.4f} {unit}')
def gradient(func, values): """Derivatives of func with respect to each value, by central differences.""" values = np.asarray(values, dtype=float) slopes = np.empty_like(values) for i, value in enumerate(values): step = 1e-6 * max(abs(value), 1.0) upper, lower = values.copy(), values.copy() upper[i] += step lower[i] -= step slopes[i] = (func(*upper) - func(*lower)) / (2 * step) return slopes def propagate(func, values, sigmas, correlation=None): """First-order propagation: the value of func and its uncertainty.""" sigmas = np.asarray(sigmas, dtype=float) if correlation is None: correlation = np.eye(len(sigmas)) covariance = np.asarray(correlation, dtype=float) * np.outer(sigmas, sigmas) slopes = gradient(func, values) return func(*values), float(np.sqrt(slopes @ covariance @ slopes)) def report(label, result, unit): """Print a labelled (value, uncertainty) pair like show does.""" print(f'{label} = {result[0]:.4f} ± {result[1]:.4f} {unit}')

For the first formula the helper must agree with EasyScience, which it does:

In [7]: Copied!

show('area_1', area_1)
report('by_helper', propagate(lambda L, W: L * W, [2.00, 1.50], [0.01, 0.01]), 'm^2') show('area_1', area_1) 
by_helper = 3.0000 ± 0.0250 m^2
area_1 = 3.0000 ± 0.0250 m^2

methods = [
    ('length and width', ['length', 'width'], lambda L, W: L * W, [2.00, 1.50]),
    ('length and perimeter', ['length', 'perimeter'], lambda L, P: L * (P / 2 - L), [2.00, 7.00]),
    (
        'length and diagonal',
        ['length', 'diagonal'],
        lambda L, D: L * np.sqrt(D**2 - L**2),
        [2.00, 2.50],
    ),
]

for label, names, func, values in methods:
    area, uncertainty = propagate(func, values, [sigma, sigma])
    slopes = gradient(func, values)
    parts = ', '.join(f'{name} {slope * sigma:+.4f}' for name, slope in zip(names, slopes))
    print(f'{label:<22} area = {area:.4f} ± {uncertainty:.4f} m^2   ({parts})')
sigma = 0.01 methods = [ ('length and width', ['length', 'width'], lambda L, W: L * W, [2.00, 1.50]), ('length and perimeter', ['length', 'perimeter'], lambda L, P: L * (P / 2 - L), [2.00, 7.00]), ( 'length and diagonal', ['length', 'diagonal'], lambda L, D: L * np.sqrt(D**2 - L**2), [2.00, 2.50], ), ] for label, names, func, values in methods: area, uncertainty = propagate(func, values, [sigma, sigma]) slopes = gradient(func, values) parts = ', '.join(f'{name} {slope * sigma:+.4f}' for name, slope in zip(names, slopes)) print(f'{label:<22} area = {area:.4f} ± {uncertainty:.4f} m^2 ({parts})') 
length and width       area = 3.0000 ± 0.0250 m^2   (length +0.0150, width +0.0200)
length and perimeter   area = 3.0000 ± 0.0112 m^2   (length -0.0050, perimeter +0.0100)
length and diagonal    area = 3.0000 ± 0.0353 m^2   (length -0.0117, diagonal +0.0333)

Measuring the length and the perimeter gives the smallest uncertainty, 0.011 m², less than half of the 0.025 m² of the obvious length-times-width. In $L\,(P/2 - L)$ a longer length also means a shorter width, so the two uses of $L$ almost cancel: the derivative with respect to $L$ is only $P/2 - 2L = -0.5$, and the uncertainty of $L$ hardly matters. The perimeter, on the other hand, enters weakly (with the factor $L/2$). The diagonal is the worst choice: $\partial A / \partial D = L D / \sqrt{D^2 - L^2} = 3.33$ makes the uncertainty of the diagonal three times as important as in a plain product.

The same measurements, with the same uncertainty each, give a result that is more or less certain depending only on the formula.

In [10]: Copied! 
diameter = Parameter(name='diameter', value=1.20, unit='m', variance=0.01**2)
circumference = Parameter(name='circumference', value=3.77, unit='m', variance=0.01**2)
diameter = Parameter(name='diameter', value=1.20, unit='m', variance=0.01**2) circumference = Parameter(name='circumference', value=3.77, unit='m', variance=0.01**2) Hint 1

The first area is np.pi * diameter**2 / 4. A plain number can multiply or divide a Parameter.

Hint 2

The relative uncertainty of $x^2$ is twice that of $x$. Compare $0.01 / 1.20$ with $0.01 / 3.77$.

Solution
area_from_diameter = np.pi * diameter**2 / 4
area_from_circumference = circumference**2 / (4 * np.pi)
show('area_from_diameter', area_from_diameter)
show('area_from_circumference', area_from_circumference)

area_from_diameter = 1.1310 ± 0.0188 m^2   in [0.0000, inf]
area_from_circumference = 1.1310 ± 0.0060 m^2   in [0.0000, inf]

The circumference gives the smaller uncertainty because 0.01 m is a smaller fraction of 3.77 m than of 1.20 m.

Hint 2

Solution

show('volume', volume)
slopes = gradient(lambda a, b, c: a * b * c, [0.50, 0.20, 0.10])
for name, slope in zip(['length', 'width', 'thickness'], slopes):

length contributes 0.00020 m^3
width contributes 0.00050 m^3

The thinnest side dominates, although all three have the same uncertainty, because 0.01 m is 10 % of 0.10 m but only 2 % of 0.50 m.

In [14]: Copied! 
by_operators = length * (perimeter / 2 - length)
show('by_operators', by_operators)
report('by_helper', propagate(lambda L, P: L * (P / 2 - L), [2.00, 7.00], [0.01, 0.01]), 'm^2')

by_operators = 3.0000 ± 0.0269 m^2
by_helper = 3.0000 ± 0.0112 m^2

EasyScience gives an uncertainty more than twice as large as the correct one. The same happens with any formula in which a measurement appears more than once, and it can go either way. A small example with a dimensionless $x = 3.0 \pm 0.1$ and $f = x\,(1 + x)$, whose derivative is $1 + 2x = 7$ and whose uncertainty should therefore be $0.7$:

In [15]: Copied! 
x = Parameter(name='x', value=3.0, variance=0.1**2)
show('x * (1 + x)', x * (1 + x))
report('by_helper', propagate(lambda x: x * (1 + x), [3.0], [0.1]), 'dimensionless')
x = Parameter(name='x', value=3.0, variance=0.1**2) show('x * (1 + x)', x * (1 + x)) report('by_helper', propagate(lambda x: x * (1 + x), [3.0], [0.1]), 'dimensionless') 
x * (1 + x) = 12.0000 ± 0.5000 dimensionless
by_helper = 12.0000 ± 0.7000 dimensionless

Three things help:

  • Where a formula uses each measurement once, the result of EasyScience is correct. Prefer such a formula if there is one, as in the round table.
  • Using the same object on both sides of one operation is fine: x * x, x**2 and x - x all have the right uncertainty.
  • Otherwise work the derivatives out, by hand or with a helper such as propagate above.
In [16]: Copied! 
plate_length = Parameter(name='plate_length', value=0.80, unit='m', variance=0.01**2)
plate_perimeter = Parameter(name='plate_perimeter', value=2.60, unit='m', variance=0.01**2)
plate_length = Parameter(name='plate_length', value=0.80, unit='m', variance=0.01**2) plate_perimeter = Parameter(name='plate_perimeter', value=2.60, unit='m', variance=0.01**2) Hint 1

The length appears twice in the formula, so EasyScience treats the two as independent.

Hint 2

propagate(lambda L, P: L * (P / 2 - L), [0.80, 2.60], [0.01, 0.01]) returns the value and the uncertainty. report prints them.

Solution
by_operators = plate_length * (plate_perimeter / 2 - plate_length)
show('by_operators', by_operators)
report('by_helper', propagate(lambda L, P: L * (P / 2 - L), [0.80, 2.60], [0.01, 0.01]), 'm^2')

Output:

by_operators = 0.4000 ± 0.0102 m^2
by_helper = 0.4000 ± 0.0050 m^2

EasyScience overestimates the uncertainty by a factor of two.

In [18]: Copied!

Hint 2

Each measurement is used once in $4\pi^2 \ell / T^2$, so the result of EasyScience is correct.

Solution
g_one_swing = 4 * np.pi**2 * pendulum_length / one_swing**2
period_ten = ten_swings / 10
g_ten_swings = 4 * np.pi**2 * pendulum_length / period_ten**2

show('g_ten_swings', g_ten_swings)

Output:

g_one_swing = 9.8696 ± 0.9872 m/s^2
g_ten_swings = 9.8696 ± 0.1007 m/s^2

Timing ten swings makes the uncertainty of g about ten times smaller.

In [20]: Copied! 
x = Parameter(name='x', value=3.0, variance=0.1**2)

same_object = x * x
two_routes = x * x - x**2
shifted = (x + 1) - x

print(f'x * x         correct {2 * 3.0 * 0.1:.4f}   EasyScience {same_object.error:.4f}')
print(f'x * x - x**2  correct {0.0:.4f}   EasyScience {two_routes.error:.4f}')
print(f'(x + 1) - x   correct {0.0:.4f}   EasyScience {shifted.error:.4f}')

x * x         correct 0.6000   EasyScience 0.6000
x * x - x**2  correct 0.0000   EasyScience 0.8485
(x + 1) - x   correct 0.0000   EasyScience 0.1414

The first uncertainty is exact. The other two quantities are exactly $0$ and $1$, with no uncertainty at all, but EasyScience reports a noticeable one.

The functions of es.math behave in the same way. The identity $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$ holds exactly, but the two terms are treated as independent:

In [21]: Copied! 
angle = Parameter(name='angle', value=0.7, unit='rad', variance=0.05**2)
identity = es.math.sin(angle) ** 2 + es.math.cos(angle) ** 2

print(f'sin² + cos²   correct {0.0:.4f}   EasyScience {identity.error:.4f}')
angle = Parameter(name='angle', value=0.7, unit='rad', variance=0.05**2) identity = es.math.sin(angle) ** 2 + es.math.cos(angle) ** 2 print(f'sin² + cos² correct {0.0:.4f} EasyScience {identity.error:.4f}') 
sin² + cos²   correct 0.0000   EasyScience 0.0697

The bounds of a Parameter are combined in the same way. Take a number between 0 and 10. Its difference with itself is always 0, but EasyScience assumes that the two sides vary independently:

In [22]: Copied! 
bounded = Parameter(name='bounded', value=4.0, variance=0.1**2, min=0.0, max=10.0)
difference = bounded - bounded

print(
    f'bounded - bounded   correct bounds [0.0, 0.0]   EasyScience [{difference.min}, {difference.max}]'
)
bounded = Parameter(name='bounded', value=4.0, variance=0.1**2, min=0.0, max=10.0) difference = bounded - bounded print( f'bounded - bounded correct bounds [0.0, 0.0] EasyScience [{difference.min}, {difference.max}]' ) 
bounded - bounded   correct bounds [0.0, 0.0]   EasyScience [-10.0, 10.0]

bounded - bounded is a special case that EasyScience recognises, so the result is exact for the uncertainty. Its bounds are still those of two independent numbers, $[0 - 10, 10 - 0]$.

When a formula uses a measurement more than once, the safest course is the one in this notebook: check the result against a short calculation with the derivatives, as propagate does.

docs.title: Three ways to find the area of a table¶
docs.text:
The top of a table is a rectangle, 2.00 m long and 1.50 m wide, so its area is 3.00 m². Suppose that you cannot measure the area directly. Every measurement with the tape measure has a standard uncertainty of ±0.01 m. You can measure the length $L$, the width $W$, the diagonal $D$ and the perimeter $P$, and the area follows from two of them in three different ways:

  1. from the length and the width: $A = L\,W$,
  2. from the length and the perimeter, because the width is $P/2 - L$: $A = L\,(P/2 - L)$,
  3. from the length and the diagonal, with Pythagoras: $A = L\,\sqrt{D^2 - L^2}$.

All three give 3.00 m². Their uncertainties are different.

docs.title: Method 1: length times width¶
docs.text: EasyScience does the work. Each measurement is used once, which is the case where its result is correct (to first order):

docs.title: A helper for any formula¶
docs.text: The other two formulas use a measurement twice, and the result of EasyScience is not correct for those (the next sections show why). To compare all three on equal terms, this notebook uses two short helpers. gradient finds the derivatives $\partial f / \partial x_i$ numerically and propagate combines them with the uncertainties exactly as in the formula above. Together with report, which prints a result like show does, they are plain Python and work for any formula:

docs.title: Methods 2 and 3, and why the formula matters¶
docs.text: The three methods side by side, each with the same tape-measure uncertainty of 0.01 m on every measurement. For each method the contribution of every measurement, $\partial A / \partial x_i \cdot \sigma_i$, is printed too:

docs.title: Exercise 1: A round table¶
docs.text: A round table top has a diameter of 1.20 ± 0.01 m. Its circumference was also measured, 3.77 ± 0.01 m. Work out the area both ways, from the diameter, $A = \pi d^2 / 4$, and from the circumference, $A = C^2 / (4\pi)$. Each measurement is used once, so the result of EasyScience is correct. Which gives the smaller uncertainty?

docs.title: Exercise 2: Which measurement matters most?¶
docs.text: A block measures 0.50 m, 0.20 m and 0.10 m, each with an uncertainty of 0.01 m. Work out its volume with its uncertainty, then print the contribution $|\partial V / \partial x_i| \cdot \sigma_i$ of each side, in m³. Which side dominates?

docs.title: When a measurement is used twice¶
docs.text: Arithmetic in EasyScience knows nothing about where its operands come from. In $L\,(P/2 - L)$ the factor $P/2 - L$ is a new number, and the multiplication by $L$ does not know that it contains $L$. It treats the two as independent, which they are not. For the table:

docs.title: Exercise 3: Length and perimeter¶
docs.text: A rectangular plate is 0.80 ± 0.01 m long and has a perimeter of 2.60 ± 0.01 m. Its area is $A = L\,(P/2 - L)$. Work out the area with EasyScience and with propagate. How different are the two uncertainties?

docs.title: Choosing the procedure¶
docs.text: Not only the formula but also the way of measuring decides the uncertainty. The period of a pendulum of length $\ell$ gives the acceleration of gravity, $g = 4\pi^2 \ell / T^2$. Because $T$ is squared, its relative uncertainty counts twice, and a timing uncertainty of 0.1 s on one swing of 2 s is 5 %. If the time of ten swings is measured instead and divided by ten, the same 0.1 s of timing uncertainty is spread over ten swings.

docs.title: Exercise 4: A pendulum¶
docs.text: A pendulum of length 1.000 ± 0.002 m is timed. One swing took 2.0 ± 0.1 s, and ten swings together took 20.0 ± 0.1 s. Work out $g$ both ways, in m/s². How much does timing ten swings help?

docs.title: Good to know¶
docs.text:
EasyScience combines numbers with the arithmetic operators and the functions of es.math, and these see only the numbers they are given, not where those numbers came from. Three consequences are worth knowing, because a wrong result looks just as confident as a right one.

The same object in one operation is recognised; the same quantity reached by two routes is not. x * x is right, but x * x - x**2 and (x + 1) - x combine intermediate results that no longer remember x. Each line gives the correct uncertainty and the one that EasyScience reports:

docs.title: Exponential and logarithm
docs.text:
This notebook covers es.math.exp, log, log10, sqrt and the error functions erf and erfc. They take a Parameter or a DescriptorNumber and return a new one with the value, unit, variance and bounds worked out: the variance to first order, the bounds as the exact range of the function over the bounds of the input.

The examples are taken from a diffraction experiment, but each one stands alone. Each part closes with a few exercises on what was just shown. Their hints and solutions are folded away and open on a click, so the text reads straight through; a solution is a worked answer with its result.

In [1]: Copied! 
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go

import easyscience as es
from easyscience import DescriptorNumber
from easyscience import Parameter
import numpy as np import plotly.graph_objects as go import easyscience as es from easyscience import DescriptorNumber from easyscience import Parameter

The function show prints a number as value, error and unit, and, for a Parameter with finite bounds, the bounds.

In [2]: Copied! 
def show(number):
    """One line with value, error, unit and, for a Parameter, the finite bounds."""
    text = f'{number.value:.4f} ± {number.error or 0.0:.4f} {number.unit}'
    if hasattr(number, 'min') and (np.isfinite(number.min) or np.isfinite(number.max)):
        text += f'   in [{number.min:.4f}, {number.max:.4f}]'
    return text
def show(number): """One line with value, error, unit and, for a Parameter, the finite bounds.""" text = f'{number.value:.4f} ± {number.error or 0.0:.4f} {number.unit}' if hasattr(number, 'min') and (np.isfinite(number.min) or np.isfinite(number.max)): text += f' in [{number.min:.4f}, {number.max:.4f}]' return text In [4]: Copied! 
q = Parameter(name='q', value=2.0, unit='1/angstrom', variance=0.02**2, min=0.5, max=4.0)
u2 = Parameter(name='u2', value=0.01, unit='angstrom**2', variance=0.002**2, min=0.0, max=0.05)

debye_waller = es.math.exp(-(q**2) * u2 / 3)
print(show(debye_waller))
q = Parameter(name='q', value=2.0, unit='1/angstrom', variance=0.02**2, min=0.5, max=4.0) u2 = Parameter(name='u2', value=0.01, unit='angstrom**2', variance=0.002**2, min=0.0, max=0.05) debye_waller = es.math.exp(-(q**2) * u2 / 3) print(show(debye_waller)) 
0.9868 ± 0.0026 dimensionless   in [0.7659, 1.0000]

The bounds are the exact range of the function over the bounds of the inputs: the factor can be as small as 0.77 and cannot exceed 1.

In [5]: Copied! 
mu = Parameter(name='mu', value=0.50, variance=0.02**2, unit='1/cm')
t = Parameter(name='t', value=2.0, variance=0.1**2, unit='cm')
mu = Parameter(name='mu', value=0.50, variance=0.02**2, unit='1/cm') t = Parameter(name='t', value=2.0, variance=0.1**2, unit='cm') Hint 1

The product of mu and t has no unit: 1/cm times cm cancels, which is why exp accepts it.

Hint 2

Write the argument first, -mu * t, and pass it to es.math.exp.

Solution
transmission = es.math.exp(-mu * t)
print(show(transmission))

Output:

0.3679 ± 0.0236 dimensionless   in [0.0000, inf]

The lower bound 0 appears because an exponential is never negative.

In [7]: Copied! 
intensity = Parameter(name='intensity', value=250.0, variance=10.0**2, min=100.0, max=400.0)
reference = DescriptorNumber(name='reference', value=1000.0, variance=0.0)

decibel = 10 * es.math.log10(intensity / reference)
print(show(decibel))

A value outside the domain is refused with an error that names the parameter:

    es.math.log10(Parameter(name='v', value=0.0, variance=0.1**2))
except ValueError as error:
    print(error)

The value of 'v' (0.0) is outside the domain (0.0, inf] of log10().

Divide the two intensities first.

Hint 2

log10 takes a dimensionless number; the factor 10 is a plain number that multiplies the result.

Solution

Output:

-6.0206 ± 0.1737 dimensionless
In [11]: Copied! 
a = Parameter(name='a', value=3.0, variance=0.1**2, min=2.0, max=4.0)
b = Parameter(name='b', value=4.0, variance=0.1**2, min=3.0, max=5.0)

5.0000 ± 0.1000 dimensionless   in [3.6056, 6.4031]

The square root of an area is a length. The square root of a length is not supported by the unit library, and is refused:

In [12]: Copied! 
area = Parameter(name='area', value=9.0, unit='m**2', variance=0.3**2, min=4.0, max=16.0)
print(show(es.math.sqrt(area)))

try:
    es.math.sqrt(Parameter(name='v', value=2.0, unit='m', variance=0.1**2))
except Exception as error:
    print(f'{type(error).__name__}: {error}')
area = Parameter(name='area', value=9.0, unit='m**2', variance=0.3**2, min=4.0, max=16.0) print(show(es.math.sqrt(area))) try: es.math.sqrt(Parameter(name='v', value=2.0, unit='m', variance=0.1**2)) except Exception as error: print(f'{type(error).__name__}: {error}')

docs.title: The exponential¶
docs.text: exp takes a dimensionless number. The Debye-Waller factor of a crystal, $\exp\!\left(-q^2\langle u^2\rangle/3\right)$, combines a scattering vector $q$ and a mean-square displacement $\langle u^2\rangle$; the units cancel, so exp accepts it:

docs.title: Exercise 1: Transmission through a sample¶
docs.text: The transmission of a beam through a sample of thickness $t$ is $T = \exp(-\mu t)$. For $\mu = 0.50 \pm 0.02$ 1/cm and $t = 2.0 \pm 0.1$ cm, what is $T$, with its uncertainty?

docs.title: Logarithms¶
docs.text: log is the natural logarithm and log10 the decimal one. Both need a dimensionless, positive number. A relative intensity in decibels uses log10; here the reference is a DescriptorNumber without an uncertainty:

docs.title: Exercise 2: Decibels¶
docs.text: A detector counts $I = 250 \pm 10$ in a run where the reference intensity is $I_0 = 1000$, taken to have no uncertainty. What is the level $10 \log_{10}(I/I_0)$ in decibels?

docs.title: The square root¶
docs.text: sqrt also accepts a number with a unit, as long as the unit can be halved. The amplitude of a vector from its two components:

docs.title: Exercise 3: Amplitude from intensity¶
docs.text: The intensity of a diffraction peak, in units of a standard, is $0.64 \pm 0.02$. Intensity is proportional to the square of the amplitude. What is the amplitude, with its uncertainty?

docs.title: The error functions¶
docs.text: The fraction of a Gaussian beam of width $\sigma$ that passes a slit of half-width $a$ is $\mathrm{erf}\!\left(a/(\sigma\sqrt{2})\right)$, and erfc $= 1 - \mathrm{erf}$ is the fraction that is blocked:

docs.title: Exercise 4: Slit transmission¶
docs.text: A Gaussian beam with $\sigma = 0.80 \pm 0.04$ mm hits a slit with a half-width of $1.0 \pm 0.05$ mm. What fraction of the beam passes?

docs.title: A round trip returns where it started¶
docs.text: The derivative of $\exp(\log x)$ is 1, so the value and the uncertainty come back unchanged:

docs.title: Charts¶
docs.text: The Debye-Waller factor falls off with $q$, and its uncertainty comes from the uncertainty of $\langle u^2\rangle = 0.010 \pm 0.002$ Å$^2$. The chart is interactive: hover over the curve to read the values. It loads Plotly from the internet, so it needs a connection. The charts are shown with a small helper, show_figure(fig), which is defined in a hidden cell; in your own notebook fig.show() does the same.

docs.title: Good to know¶
docs.text: The first-order variance ignores the curvature of the function, so it is accurate only while the uncertainty of the argument is small compared with the distance over which the slope changes. For $x \sim \mathcal{N}(1, 1)$ the first-order variance of $\exp(x)$ is $e^2 = 7.389$, but the exact variance of $\exp(x)$ is $e^3(e - 1) = 34.51$:

docs.title: Hyperbolic functions
docs.text:
This notebook covers es.math.sinh, cosh, tanh and their inverses arcsinh, arccosh and arctanh. They take a dimensionless Parameter or DescriptorNumber and return a new one with the value, variance and bounds worked out: the variance to first order, the bounds as the exact range of the function over the bounds of the input.

The examples are taken from a diffraction experiment, but each one stands alone. Each part closes with a few exercises on what was just shown. Their hints and solutions are folded away and open on a click, so the text reads straight through; a solution is a worked answer with its result.

In [1]: Copied!

The function show prints a number as value, error and unit, and, for a Parameter with finite bounds, the bounds.

In [2]: Copied! 
def show(number):
    """One line with value, error, unit and, for a Parameter, the finite bounds."""
    text = f'{number.value:.4f} ± {number.error or 0.0:.4f} {number.unit}'
    if hasattr(number, 'min') and (np.isfinite(number.min) or np.isfinite(number.max)):
        text += f'   in [{number.min:.4f}, {number.max:.4f}]'
    return text
def show(number): """One line with value, error, unit and, for a Parameter, the finite bounds.""" text = f'{number.value:.4f} ± {number.error or 0.0:.4f} {number.unit}' if hasattr(number, 'min') and (np.isfinite(number.min) or np.isfinite(number.max)): text += f' in [{number.min:.4f}, {number.max:.4f}]' return text In [4]: Copied!

docs.title: sinh, cosh and tanh¶
docs.text:
The three functions are monotonic or have one minimum, so their bounds are exact:

  • sinh rises from $-\infty$ to $\infty$,
  • cosh has its minimum 1 at 0 and is symmetric,
  • tanh rises from $-1$ to $1$.

docs.title: Exercise 1: Saturation of a magnet¶
docs.text: A magnetisation follows $\tanh(x)$ with $x = 0.80 \pm 0.05$. The fitting range of $x$ is 0 to 3. What is the magnetisation, and between which values can it lie?

docs.title: The inverse functions¶
docs.text:
arcsinh accepts any number, arccosh needs a number of at least 1, and arctanh a number between -1 and

  1. The inverse of tanh turns a measured saturation back into the argument that produced it:

docs.title: Exercise 2: Recovering the argument¶
docs.text: A magnet reaches $0.50 \pm 0.02$ of its saturation magnetisation, and the magnetisation follows $\tanh(x)$. What is $x$?

docs.title: Bounds that are not at the ends¶
docs.text: The hyperbolic cosine has its minimum at 0, in the middle of an interval that contains 0. The lower bound of the result is therefore 1, not the value at either end:

docs.title: Exercise 3: The lowest value of cosh¶
docs.text: A parameter can vary between -1 and 1, and its current value is 0.5 ± 0.05. What is the lowest value that cosh of it can take? Print only that number.

docs.title: Values outside the domain¶
docs.text: arccosh is only defined for numbers of at least 1. A value outside the domain is refused with an error that names the parameter, as the next exercise shows.

docs.title: Exercise 4: Outside the domain¶
docs.text: Predict what es.math.arccosh does with $x = 0.5 \pm 0.01$, then try it. Catch the error and print its message.

docs.title: A round trip¶
docs.text: Each function undoes its inverse, with the value and the uncertainty unchanged:

docs.title: Charts¶
docs.text: The magnetisation $\tanh(x)$ and its uncertainty for $x$ with an uncertainty of 0.2. The band is widest where the curve is steepest, near 0, and vanishes as the curve saturates. The chart is interactive: hover over the curve to read the values. It loads Plotly from the internet, so it needs a connection. The charts are shown with a small helper, show_figure(fig), which is defined in a hidden cell; in your own notebook fig.show() does the same.

docs.title: Good to know¶
docs.text: At the minimum of cosh the derivative is 0, so the first-order variance is 0, however large the uncertainty of the input is. For an input $0 \pm 0.5$ the exact variance of $\cosh(x)$, with $x \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.5^2)$, is $\tfrac{1}{2}(1 + e^{2\sigma^2}) - e^{\sigma^2} = 0.0403$:

docs.title: Inverse trigonometric functions
docs.text:
This notebook covers es.math.arcsin, arccos, arctan and arctan2. They take a Parameter or a DescriptorNumber and return an angle, in radians by default; the keyword unit='deg' returns degrees, with the variance and the bounds converted to match. The variance is propagated to first order, and the bounds are the exact range of the function over the bounds of the input.

The examples are taken from a diffraction experiment, but each one stands alone. Each part closes with a few exercises on what was just shown. Their hints and solutions are folded away and open on a click, so the text reads straight through; a solution is a worked answer with its result.

def show(number):
    """One line with value, error, unit and, for a Parameter, the finite bounds."""
    text = f'{number.value:.4f} ± {number.error or 0.0:.4f} {number.unit}'
    if hasattr(number, 'min') and (np.isfinite(number.min) or np.isfinite(number.max)):
        text += f'   in [{number.min:.4f}, {number.max:.4f}]'
    return text
def show(number): """One line with value, error, unit and, for a Parameter, the finite bounds.""" text = f'{number.value:.4f} ± {number.error or 0.0:.4f} {number.unit}' if hasattr(number, 'min') and (np.isfinite(number.min) or np.isfinite(number.max)): text += f' in [{number.min:.4f}, {number.max:.4f}]' return text In [4]: Copied!

docs.title: The arcsine and the Bragg angle¶
docs.text: Bragg's law $\lambda = 2d\sin\theta$ gives the Bragg angle from the lattice spacing $d$ and the wavelength $\lambda$, with $\theta = \arcsin\!\left(\lambda/(2d)\right)$. The argument is dimensionless because the two lengths cancel:

docs.text: arccos returns an angle between $0$ and $\pi$, and arctan an angle between $-\pi/2$ and $\pi/2$. The arccosine of a number between 0 and 1:

docs.title: The two-argument arctangent¶
docs.text: arctan(b / a) cannot tell $(a, b)$ from $(-a, -b)$. arctan2(b, a) uses the signs of both arguments to find the right quadrant. The phase of a structure factor $F = a + \mathrm{i}\,b$ is arctan2(b, a); the two arguments must have the same unit (here none):

docs.title: Values outside the domain¶
docs.text: arcsin and arccos accept numbers between -1 and 1 only. A ratio $\lambda/(2d)$ larger than 1 means that no angle satisfies Bragg's law for that wavelength and spacing, and the function says so instead of returning a meaningless number. The error message names the parameter it was given.

docs.text: The sine and the arcsine undo each other. The Bragg angle recovered from $d$ and $\lambda$ is the angle we started with, and its error is almost the same:

This notebook covers es.math.sin, cos, tan and sinc. They take a Parameter or a DescriptorNumber and return a new one with the value, unit, variance and bounds worked out: the variance to first order, the bounds as the exact range of the function over the bounds of the input.

Their hints and solutions are folded away and open on a click, so the text reads straight through; a solution is a worked answer with its result.

docs.title: Angles need a unit¶
docs.text: The argument of sin, cos and tan must have an angle unit, rad or deg, and the result is dimensionless. A length is refused:

docs.title: The sine and Bragg's law¶
docs.text:
Bragg's law relates the spacing $d$ of the lattice planes to the Bragg angle $\theta$ and the wavelength $\lambda$, and the scattering vector is $q$:

$$ d = \frac{\lambda}{2\sin\theta}, \qquad q = \frac{4\pi\sin\theta}{\lambda}. $$

The uncertainty is converted correctly: $\sin 15^\circ$ has an error of $\cos 15^\circ \times \sigma_\theta$ with $\sigma_\theta$ in radians. The wavelength is a measured constant, so it is a DescriptorNumber (no bounds); the angle may be fitted, so it is a Parameter:

docs.title: Exercise 1: Scattering vector¶
docs.text: X-rays of wavelength 1.54 Å (taken to have no uncertainty) are scattered at the Bragg angle $\theta = 22.5 \pm 0.2^\circ$. The scattering vector is $q = 4\pi\sin\theta/\lambda$. What is $q$?

docs.title: Exercise 2: Lattice spacing¶
docs.text: For the same measurement, $\theta = 22.5 \pm 0.2^\circ$ and $\lambda = 1.54$ Å, what is the lattice spacing $d = \lambda/(2\sin\theta)$?

docs.title: The cosine and the tangent¶
docs.text: The same rules apply. The tangent of an angle whose bounds reach $90^\circ$ has no upper limit:

docs.title: Exercise 3: Position of a spot¶
docs.text: A flat detector is 1.50 ± 0.01 m from the sample. A beam scattered by $2\theta = 30.0 \pm 0.2^\circ$ hits it at a height $y = L\tan(2\theta)$ above the direct beam. What is $y$?

docs.title: The sinc function¶
docs.text: sinc(x) is $\sin(x)/x$, not the normalised $\sin(\pi x)/(\pi x)$ of NumPy. It takes radians or a dimensionless number, and refuses degrees. The intensity of single-slit diffraction is proportional to $\mathrm{sinc}^2$:

docs.title: Exercise 4: Single-slit intensity¶
docs.text: The intensity of single-slit diffraction, relative to the central maximum, is $\mathrm{sinc}^2(x)$. What is it at $x = 2.0 \pm 0.1$?

docs.title: Exact bounds¶
docs.text: The bounds of the input carry through. The sine of an angle that may vary between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$ reaches 1 in the middle, so the upper bound of the result is exactly 1, not the sine of either end:

docs.title: Charts¶
docs.text: The lattice spacing $d(\theta)$ of the Bragg example, for an angle with an uncertainty of $1^\circ$ (ten times larger than above, so that the band can be seen). The band is widest at small angles: the relative error of $d$ is $\cot\theta\,\sigma_\theta$. The chart is interactive: hover over the curve to read the values. It loads Plotly from the internet, so it needs a connection. The charts are shown with a small helper, show_figure(fig), which is defined in a hidden cell; in your own notebook fig.show() does the same.

docs.title: Good to know¶
docs.text: The two curves agree to within a few per cent away from the extremes. At $\pi/2$ and $3\pi/2$ the sine is flat, its derivative is 0, and the first-order error drops to (almost) zero, while the Monte Carlo error stays near $\sigma^2/\sqrt{2}\approx 0.06$:

docs.title: Fitting
docs.text: A fit starts from data and a model and returns the model parameters with their uncertainties. These notebooks show how to fit with EasyScience and, above all, what to do with the result: derived quantities with their uncertainties, computed with the arithmetic and the functions of es.math. They assume that you know the Basics.

docs.title: A suggested path
docs.text:
• Fitting introduction – Fit a straight line to simulated data, then work out quantities that follow from the fitted slope. Start here.
  • SANS sphere – Fit the scattering of spheres to small-angle neutron scattering data, then derive the diameter, the volume, the radius of gyration and a Guinier approximation. Next.
  • QENS Lorentzian – Fit a Lorentzian, convolved with the instrument resolution, to quasi-elastic neutron scattering data, then derive the relaxation time, a decay curve and the resolution. Next.
  • Bayesian QENS – Sample the posterior of the QENS model and compare its derived quantities with the first-order uncertainties. Advanced. For the sampling workflow itself, with diagnostics and extending a chain, see Bayesian analysis in Advanced Topics.

docs.title: How the notebooks work
docs.text:
• Each part ends with a few exercises. The hints and the solution are folded away and open on a click, so you can read straight through or try each exercise first.
  • A solution is a worked answer: its code runs and the result is shown.
  • The SANS and QENS notebooks download their data the first time they run, so they need an internet connection. So do the interactive charts.
  • Each notebook can be downloaded and run on your computer; see how to run the tutorials.

docs.title: Bayesian QENS
docs.text:
A least-squares fit reports one best value and one symmetric uncertainty for each parameter. A Bayesian analysis reports the whole posterior distribution: how probable each combination of parameter values is, given the data. This notebook samples the posterior of a QENS model with the DREAM algorithm, and then compares two ways of getting the uncertainty of a quantity that is derived from the parameters: the first-order propagation of es.math, and the posterior itself.

The model and the data are those of the notebook on fitting QENS data with a Lorentzian, which is the better place to start. Each part here closes with a few exercises on what was just shown. Their hints and solutions are folded away and open on a click, so the text reads straight through; a solution is a worked answer with its result.

The model is a Lorentzian with area $A$, half width $\gamma$ and centre $\omega_0$, convolved with a Gaussian resolution of width $\sigma$. The min and max of every parameter are not only the range of a fit: for the sampler they define a uniform prior, so the sampler only visits values inside the range.

class Quasielastic(ModelBase):
    """A Lorentzian convolved with a Gaussian resolution, as a function of the energy transfer."""

    def __init__(self, area: float, gamma: float, omega_0: float, sigma: float):
        super().__init__()
        self._area = Parameter(name='area', value=area, min=0.01, max=100)
        self._gamma = Parameter(name='gamma', value=gamma, unit='meV', min=1e-4, max=1e-2)
        self._omega_0 = Parameter(name='omega_0', value=omega_0, unit='meV', min=0, max=2e-3)
        self._sigma = Parameter(name='sigma', value=sigma, unit='meV', min=1e-5, max=1e-1)

    @property
    def area(self) -> Parameter:
        return self._area

    @property
    def gamma(self) -> Parameter:
        return self._gamma

    @property
    def omega_0(self) -> Parameter:
        return self._omega_0

    @property
    def sigma(self) -> Parameter:
        return self._sigma

    def __call__(self, omega):
        width = self._gamma.value
        lorentzian = (
            self._area.value / np.pi * width / ((omega - self._omega_0.value) ** 2 + width**2)
        )
        resolution = norm(0, self._sigma.value).pdf(omega)
        resolution /= resolution.sum()
        return np.convolve(lorentzian, resolution, 'same')
class Quasielastic(ModelBase): """A Lorentzian convolved with a Gaussian resolution, as a function of the energy transfer.""" def __init__(self, area: float, gamma: float, omega_0: float, sigma: float): super().__init__() self._area = Parameter(name='area', value=area, min=0.01, max=100) self._gamma = Parameter(name='gamma', value=gamma, unit='meV', min=1e-4, max=1e-2) self._omega_0 = Parameter(name='omega_0', value=omega_0, unit='meV', min=0, max=2e-3) self._sigma = Parameter(name='sigma', value=sigma, unit='meV', min=1e-5, max=1e-1) @property def area(self) -> Parameter: return self._area @property def gamma(self) -> Parameter: return self._gamma @property def omega_0(self) -> Parameter: return self._omega_0 @property def sigma(self) -> Parameter: return self._sigma def __call__(self, omega): width = self._gamma.value lorentzian = ( self._area.value / np.pi * width / ((omega - self._omega_0.value) ** 2 + width**2) ) resolution = norm(0, self._sigma.value).pdf(omega) resolution /= resolution.sum() return np.convolve(lorentzian, resolution, 'same') In [5]: Copied!

Before the draws are used, the chains have to be checked for convergence. The Gelman-Rubin statistic $\hat{R}$ compares the variation within each chain with the variation between chains. Values close to 1 mean that the chains agree: below 1.1 is acceptable and below 1.01 is strict. If a value is higher, draw more samples:

docs.title: Bayesian fitting of QENS data: from the posterior to derived quantities¶
The data and the model¶
docs.text: The data are simulated and reduced QENS intensities, as in the notebook on fitting QENS data, for the energy transfer $\omega$ in meV, cropped to $|\omega| < 0.06$ meV:

docs.title: Start from a fit¶
docs.text: The sampler starts its chains close to the current parameter values, so it is worth fitting first. The fit also gives the reference for the comparison below: a value and a first-order uncertainty for every parameter. The sampler moves the parameters while it works, so the fitted numbers are kept in separate DescriptorNumbers:

docs.title: Sampling the posterior¶
docs.text: DREAM is an ensemble Markov-chain Monte Carlo method: many chains explore the parameter space in parallel and exchange information. The sampler takes the configured fitter, the data and the weights, and returns the draws. The sampler requires a Bumps minimizer, so the fitter is switched to it first. The run takes a few tens of seconds.

docs.title: A derived quantity from the draws¶
docs.text: Every draw is a possible set of parameters, so a derived quantity can be computed for every draw. The distribution of the results is the posterior of that quantity, with no approximation. The relaxation time is $\tau = \hbar/\gamma$. On the draws this is plain NumPy, because es.math takes one Parameter at a time. The first-order propagation of es.math starts from the fitted value:

docs.title: Exercise 1: The half-life from the posterior¶
docs.text: The intermediate scattering function falls to one half at $t_{1/2} = \tau \ln 2$. Work out $t_{1/2}$ for every draw, print its median and its central 68 % interval, and print the first-order value from the fitted width for comparison.

docs.title: A poorly determined parameter¶
docs.text: The resolution width $\sigma$ is known much less well than $\gamma$. A quantity that depends on its inverse, such as the coherence time $\hbar/\sigma$ that belongs to the resolution width, is a strongly non-linear function of it. The first-order uncertainty is symmetric, while the posterior is not:

docs.title: Exercise 2: A quantity that is linear¶
docs.text: The resolution full width at half maximum, $2\sqrt{2\ln 2}\;\sigma$, is proportional to $\sigma$. Print the standard deviation of its draws, in µeV, and the first-order uncertainty from es.math.

docs.title: Exercise 3: How likely is a coarse resolution?¶
docs.text: Count the fraction of the draws in which the resolution full width at half maximum, $2\sqrt{2\ln 2}\;\sigma$, is larger than 3 µeV. Print it as a percentage. This is the posterior probability of the statement.

docs.title: Good to know¶
docs.text:
• The draws change from run to run. DREAM is a random algorithm, so the numbers differ a little every time the notebook runs. Increasing samples makes them more stable, and the convergence check above says whether they can be trusted.
  • es.math is for fitted values; NumPy is for draws. es.math works on one Parameter at a time and gives a first-order, symmetric uncertainty. For a quantity that is nearly linear in well-determined parameters it is a quick and accurate shortcut. For a strongly non-linear quantity of a poorly determined parameter, compute it on the draws.
  • The sampler moves the parameters. After sampling, model.gamma.value is no longer the fitted value. That is why the fitted numbers were copied to fitted first.

docs.title: Fitting introduction
docs.text:
A fit returns parameters with an uncertainty: the same Parameter objects used in the basics tutorials on maths. This notebook fits a straight line to simulated data and then computes quantities that derive from the fitted parameters, with their uncertainty, using ordinary arithmetic and es.math.

def show(number):
    """One line with value, error, unit and, for a Parameter, the finite bounds."""
    text = f'{number.value:.4f} ± {number.error or 0.0:.4f} {number.unit}'
    if hasattr(number, 'min') and (np.isfinite(number.min) or np.isfinite(number.max)):
        text += f'   in [{number.min:.4f}, {number.max:.4f}]'
    return text
def show(number): """One line with value, error, unit and, for a Parameter, the finite bounds.""" text = f'{number.value:.4f} ± {number.error or 0.0:.4f} {number.unit}' if hasattr(number, 'min') and (np.isfinite(number.min) or np.isfinite(number.max)): text += f' in [{number.min:.4f}, {number.max:.4f}]' return text In [4]: Copied! 
class StraightLine(ModelBase):
    """A straight line, y = slope * x + intercept."""

    def __init__(self, slope: float, intercept: float):
        super().__init__()
        self._slope = Parameter(name='slope', value=slope)
        self._intercept = Parameter(name='intercept', value=intercept)

    @property
    def slope(self) -> Parameter:
        return self._slope

    @property
    def intercept(self) -> Parameter:
        return self._intercept

    def __call__(self, x):
        return self._slope.value * x + self._intercept.value
class StraightLine(ModelBase): """A straight line, y = slope * x + intercept.""" def __init__(self, slope: float, intercept: float): super().__init__() self._slope = Parameter(name='slope', value=slope) self._intercept = Parameter(name='intercept', value=intercept) @property def slope(self) -> Parameter: return self._slope @property def intercept(self) -> Parameter: return self._intercept def __call__(self, x): return self._slope.value * x + self._intercept.value In [5]: Copied!

The same works with the functions of es.math. The angle of the line with the $x$ axis is the arctangent of the slope:

In [9]: Copied!

One caution. The slope and the intercept of one fit are correlated, but arithmetic treats numbers as independent. A quantity that depends on both, such as the $x$ where the line crosses zero, $-\text{intercept}/\text{slope}$, therefore has an error that cannot be fully trusted. A quantity that depends on one parameter, as in the exercises below, is fine.

docs.title: Introduction to fitting: from fitted parameters to derived quantities¶
The model¶
docs.text: A model is a class that holds its fit parameters as Parameters and is callable with the independent variable. Inside the call, use plain NumPy on the .value of each parameter: the fitting engine calls it many times with plain numbers. The es.math functions belong after the fit, on the fitted parameters.

docs.title: Simulated data and the fit¶
docs.text: The data follow $y = 0.6\,x + 1.0$ with Gaussian noise of 0.3. The weights are $1/\sigma$ of each point:

docs.title: Quantities that derive from the fit¶
docs.text: The fitted parameters can be used like any other number with an uncertainty. A line through the origin with the slope would reach $y = 6$ at $x = 10$:

docs.title: QENS Lorentzian
docs.text:
Quasi-elastic neutron scattering (QENS) measures small energy exchanges between neutrons and a sample. A broadening of the elastic line, described by a Lorentzian, reveals how fast the atoms or molecules move. This notebook fits a Lorentzian, convolved with the resolution of the instrument, to reduced QENS data, and then works out quantities that follow from the fit, such as the relaxation time, with their uncertainty, using the arithmetic and the functions of es.math.

Each part closes with a few exercises on what was just shown. Their hints and solutions are folded away and open on a click, so the text reads straight through; a solution is a worked answer with its result.

class Quasielastic(ModelBase):
    """A Lorentzian convolved with a Gaussian resolution, as a function of the energy transfer."""

    def __init__(self, area: float, gamma: float, omega_0: float, sigma: float):
        super().__init__()
        self._area = Parameter(name='area', value=area, min=0.01, max=100)
        self._gamma = Parameter(name='gamma', value=gamma, unit='meV', min=1e-4, max=1e-2)
        self._omega_0 = Parameter(name='omega_0', value=omega_0, unit='meV', min=0, max=2e-3)
        self._sigma = Parameter(name='sigma', value=sigma, unit='meV', min=1e-5, max=1e-1)

    @property
    def area(self) -> Parameter:
        return self._area

    @property
    def gamma(self) -> Parameter:
        return self._gamma

    @property
    def omega_0(self) -> Parameter:
        return self._omega_0

    @property
    def sigma(self) -> Parameter:
        return self._sigma

    def __call__(self, omega):
        width = self._gamma.value
        lorentzian = (
            self._area.value / np.pi * width / ((omega - self._omega_0.value) ** 2 + width**2)
        )
        resolution = norm(0, self._sigma.value).pdf(omega)
        resolution /= resolution.sum()
        return np.convolve(lorentzian, resolution, 'same')

  • The uncertainty is symmetric and first order. For a quantity that is a strongly non-linear function of a poorly determined parameter, such as $\hbar/\sigma$, a symmetric uncertainty can be misleading. The Bayesian notebook compares it with the full posterior. It also shows that $\gamma$ and $\sigma$ are correlated, which the arithmetic of EasyScience ignores.

docs.title: Fitting QENS data with a Lorentzian¶
The data¶
docs.text: The data are simulated and reduced intensities $I(\omega)$ with their uncertainties, as a function of the energy transfer $\omega$ in meV. They are stored in a plain text file with three columns, which is downloaded once and then read from the local copy. Only the region around the elastic line, $|\omega| < 0.06$ meV, is kept:

docs.title: The model¶
docs.text:
QENS data are usually described by a Lorentzian,

$$ L(\omega) = \frac{A\,\gamma}{\pi\left[(\omega - \omega_0)^2 + \gamma^2\right]}, $$

where $A$ is the area, $\gamma$ the half width at half maximum and $\omega_0$ a small offset of the centre. The instrument blurs the line, which is modelled by convolving it with a Gaussian of width $\sigma$. The model has four parameters. The widths and the offset are energies, so they carry the unit meV.

Inside __call__ the model works with plain NumPy arrays and the .value of each parameter: es.math takes one Parameter at a time, so it belongs after the fit, on the fitted parameters.

docs.title: The fit¶
docs.text: The fit starts from a rough guess. The weights are the inverse uncertainties of the points. After the fit each parameter holds its fitted value and its uncertainty:

docs.title: From a width to a time¶
docs.text: The width $\gamma$ of the Lorentzian is the inverse of a relaxation time, $\tau = \hbar/\gamma$. The reduced Planck constant in meV·ps is a constant without uncertainty, so it is a DescriptorNumber. The units of meV*ps and meV cancel to give a time, and the uncertainty of $\gamma$ is carried along:

docs.title: Exercise 1: The half-life of the decay¶
docs.text: The intermediate scattering function falls to one half at $t_{1/2} = \tau \ln 2$. Work out $t_{1/2}$ for the fitted width, in ps, with its uncertainty.

docs.title: Exercise 2: The decay after 50 ps¶
docs.text: Work out the intermediate scattering function $I(t)$ at $t = 50$ ps for the fitted width, with its uncertainty.

docs.title: The line width and the resolution¶
docs.text: The full width at half maximum of the Lorentzian is $\Gamma = 2\gamma$, and its peak height, before the blurring by the instrument, is $A/(\pi\gamma)$. The Gaussian resolution has the full width at half maximum $2\sqrt{2\ln 2}\;\sigma$. With the constant wrapped in a DescriptorNumber, es.math.sqrt and es.math.log give it with its uncertainty, which convert_unit expresses in µeV:

docs.title: Exercise 3: The height of the line¶
docs.text: The peak height of the Lorentzian, before the blurring by the resolution, is $A/(\pi\gamma)$. Work it out with its uncertainty.

docs.title: Exercise 4: Resolution against line width¶
docs.text: Work out the ratio of the resolution FWHM to the line width $\Gamma = 2\gamma$, with its uncertainty. Is the line broader than the resolution?

docs.title: Good to know¶
docs.text: • Constants have to be wrapped. es.math accepts a Parameter or a DescriptorNumber, not a plain number, and it takes one value at a time, not an array. That is why the model uses NumPy and the results use es.math:

docs.title: SANS sphere
docs.text:
Small-angle neutron scattering (SANS) measures how a sample scatters neutrons at small angles. The shape of the curve $I(q)$ carries the size and shape of the objects in the sample. This notebook fits a model of spheres to reduced SANS data, and then goes one step further: it works out physical quantities that follow from the fitted radius, with their uncertainty, using the arithmetic and the functions of es.math.

Each part closes with a few exercises on what was just shown. Their hints and solutions are folded away and open on a click, so the text reads straight through; a solution is a worked answer with its result.

class Sphere(ModelBase):
    """The scattering of identical spheres, as a function of q."""

    def __init__(self, scale: float, delta_rho: float, r: float, bkg: float):
        super().__init__()
        self._scale = Parameter(name='scale', value=scale, fixed=True)
        self._delta_rho = Parameter(
            name='delta_rho', value=delta_rho, unit='1/angstrom**2', min=0, max=10
        )
        self._r = Parameter(name='r', value=r, unit='angstrom', min=10, max=1000)
        self._bkg = Parameter(name='bkg', value=bkg, min=1e-3, max=1e-1)

    @property
    def scale(self) -> Parameter:
        return self._scale

    @property
    def delta_rho(self) -> Parameter:
        return self._delta_rho

    @property
    def r(self) -> Parameter:
        return self._r

    @property
    def bkg(self) -> Parameter:
        return self._bkg

    def __call__(self, q):
        qr = q * self._r.value
        volume = 4 / 3 * np.pi * self._r.value**3
        form_factor = 3 * volume * self._delta_rho.value * (np.sin(qr) - qr * np.cos(qr)) / qr**3
        return self._scale.value / volume * form_factor**2 + self._bkg.value

docs.title: Fitting SANS data with a sphere¶
The data¶
docs.text: The data are simulated and reduced SANS intensities $I(q)$ with their uncertainties, for the scattering vector $q$ in $\text{Å}^{-1}$. They are stored in a plain text file with three columns, which is downloaded once and then read from the local copy:

docs.title: The model¶
docs.text:
For a dilute sample of identical spheres of radius $r$ the intensity is

$$ I(q) = \frac{\text{scale}}{V}\left(\frac{3V\,\Delta\rho\,[\sin(qr) - qr\cos(qr)]}{(qr)^3}\right)^2 + \text{bkg}, \qquad V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3, $$

where $\Delta\rho$ is the contrast between the spheres and the solvent and $\text{bkg}$ is a flat background. The scale factor is known from the instrument and stays fixed, so the fit has three free parameters: $\Delta\rho$, $r$ and $\text{bkg}$.

A model is a class that holds its parameters as Parameters and is called with $q$. The parameters carry units, so that results derived from them have units too. Inside __call__ the model works with plain NumPy arrays and the .value of each parameter: es.math takes one Parameter at a time, so it belongs after the fit, on the fitted parameters.

docs.title: The fit¶
docs.text: The fit starts from a rough guess. The weights are the inverse uncertainties of the points. After the fit each parameter holds its fitted value and its uncertainty:

docs.title: Size and volume¶
docs.text: The fitted radius is a Parameter with the unit $\text{Å}$ and an uncertainty. Ordinary arithmetic gives the diameter and the volume, and convert_unit expresses them in nanometres. The uncertainty is carried along and converted with the value:

docs.title: Exercise 1: Surface of the sphere¶
docs.text: The surface area of a sphere is $4\pi r^2$. Work out the surface area of the fitted sphere in $\text{nm}^2$, with its uncertainty.

docs.title: The radius of gyration¶
docs.text: The radius of gyration $R_g$ describes how the scattering mass is spread around the centre. For a uniform sphere $R_g = \sqrt{3/5}\;r$. A constant such as $3/5$ has to be wrapped in a DescriptorNumber before es.math accepts it:

docs.title: Exercise 2: The first minimum¶
docs.text: The form factor of a sphere has its first minimum where $qr = 4.4934$. Work out the $q$ of the first minimum for the fitted radius, in $\text{Å}^{-1}$, and the length $2\pi/q$ that belongs to it.

docs.title: The Guinier approximation¶
docs.text: At small $q$ the scattering of any object falls off as $I(q)/I(0) \approx \exp(-q^2 R_g^2/3)$ (the Guinier approximation). With es.math.exp, the value at a given $q$ comes with an uncertainty from $R_g$. The exponent has to be dimensionless: $q$ in $\text{Å}^{-1}$ times $R_g$ in $\text{Å}$ is:

docs.title: Exercise 3: Guinier at another q¶
docs.text: Work out the Guinier value $I(q)/I(0)$ at $q = 0.03\ \text{Å}^{-1}$ for the fitted sphere, with its uncertainty. Then print the exact sphere value at the same $q$ for comparison.

docs.title: Exercise 4: Where the Guinier curve reaches 1/e¶
docs.text: The Guinier curve reaches $1/e$ where $q R_g = \sqrt{3}$. Work out that $q$ for the fitted sphere, with its uncertainty, in $\text{Å}^{-1}$.

docs.title: Good to know¶
docs.text: • The functions of angles need an angle unit. The product $qr$ is dimensionless, so the full sphere amplitude $\sin(qr) - qr\cos(qr)$ cannot be evaluated with es.math.sin and es.math.cos directly: they ask for rad or deg, while es.math.sinc accepts a dimensionless number.

docs.title: Workshops & Schools
docs.text:
These notebooks come from workshops and schools. They walk through the whole analysis of one data set, from loading the reduced data to the fit, and are written as exercises for a group.

  • Fitting QENS – Fit a quasi-elastic neutron scattering (QENS) data set with EasyScience.
  • Fitting SANS – Fit a small-angle neutron scattering (SANS) data set with EasyScience.

The Fitting section covers the same data sets with model classes and units, and shows how to derive quantities from the fit.

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text:
• Concepts – What a Parameter and a DescriptorNumber are, how uncertainties, bounds and units are handled, and how models and fits fit together.
  • Controlling Log Output – How to suppress, filter, or redirect the messages that EasyScience produces. Covers the EASYSCIENCE_LOG_LEVEL environment variable, the logger hierarchy, context managers, and common recipes.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text: EasyScience works with numbers that know what they are: a value, a unit, an uncertainty and, for numbers that are fitted, the range they may take. This page defines the ideas that the tutorials rely on.

docs.title: Numbers with a unit and an uncertainty
docs.text:
A DescriptorNumber is a number with a value, a unit and an uncertainty. It takes part in arithmetic and in the functions of es.math, but it cannot be fitted. It is the right choice for a constant, or for a measured value that no fit will touch.

A Parameter is a DescriptorNumber that can be fitted. It adds two things: bounds and a fixed/free switch. A free parameter is varied by a fit; a fixed one is not.

The uncertainty is stored as a variance, in the square of the unit. The attribute error is its square root, in the unit itself. The arithmetic notebook explains the difference between an error and an uncertainty.

The bounds min and max are the range that a fit may explore. For Bayesian sampling the same range is the uniform prior of the parameter.

Units are checked. Numbers whose units have different dimensions cannot be added, a length and a time for example, while a length in metres and one in centimetres can: the result takes the unit of the first. A product or a quotient gets the combined unit, and convert_unit expresses a number, with its uncertainty and bounds, in another unit.

docs.title: Results of calculations
docs.text:
Arithmetic and the functions of es.math return a new number. Its value, unit, uncertainty and bounds are worked out from the numbers that went in. The uncertainty is propagated to first order and assumes that the inputs are independent. Two consequences follow:

  • a result is a snapshot: it does not change when a number it came from changes afterwards,
  • a quantity that depends on the same number more than once, or on correlated numbers, can have an unreliable uncertainty. The notebooks on error propagation and correlation show when and by how much.

docs.title: Models and fitting
docs.text:
A model is a class derived from ModelBase that holds its parameters as properties and is called with the independent variable. A Fitter takes the model and finds the free parameters that make it describe the data. The available minimizers are LMFit, Bumps and DFO, selected with AvailableMinimizers.

After a fit every free parameter holds its fitted value and its uncertainty, and can be used like any other number. A Sampler explores the full posterior distribution of the parameters instead of a single best value.

The Fitting tutorials show all of this on data.

docs.title: Controlling Log Output
docs.text: EasyScience uses Python's standard logging module for all informational and warning messages. This gives you full control over what output the library produces and where it goes.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
The most common operation is suppressing all EasyScience messages. You can do it in one line:

from easyscience import global_object

global_object.log.level = 'ERROR'

Or using the standard library directly:

import logging

logging.getLogger('easyscience').setLevel(logging.ERROR)

Both forms set the package-root logger to ERROR, which suppresses all WARNING, INFO, and DEBUG messages from EasyScience.

docs.title: Logger Hierarchy
docs.text:
EasyScience loggers are named hierarchically under the root easyscience logger. This lets you suppress the whole package or individual subsystems:

easyscience                        # root — controls everything
├── easyscience.base_classes       # EasyList runtime warnings
├── easyscience.legacy             # ObjBase / CollectionBase deprecations
├── easyscience.deprecated         # @deprecated decorator messages
├── easyscience.fitting            # import-availability warnings
│   ├── easyscience.fitting.bumps  # Bumps fitting runtime messages
│   ├── easyscience.fitting.lmfit  # LMFit fitting runtime messages
│   └── easyscience.fitting.dfo    # DFO fitting runtime messages
├── easyscience.variable           # parameter warnings
└── easyscience.global_object      # undo/redo, debugging diagnostics

Setting the level on a parent logger affects all its children, because child loggers inherit the parent's effective level.

import logging

# Suppress everything from the fitting subsystem (including bumps/lmfit/dfo)
logging.getLogger('easyscience.fitting').setLevel(logging.ERROR)

# Suppress only Bumps runtime messages
logging.getLogger('easyscience.fitting.bumps').setLevel(logging.ERROR)

# Suppress only legacy deprecation notices
logging.getLogger('easyscience.legacy').setLevel(logging.ERROR)

docs.title: Environment Variable
docs.text:
You can control the log level before importing EasyScience by setting the EASYSCIENCE_LOG_LEVEL environment variable. This is useful when a downstream library cannot configure logging in code before EasyScience is imported.

Accepted values: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL, or a numeric level (e.g. 40).

Example — suppressing all import-time messages:

# Windows PowerShell
$env:EASYSCIENCE_LOG_LEVEL = 'ERROR'
python -c "import easyscience"  # silent

# Linux / macOS
EASYSCIENCE_LOG_LEVEL=ERROR python -c "import easyscience"  # silent

Or from Python, set the environment variable before the import:

import os

os.environ['EASYSCIENCE_LOG_LEVEL'] = 'ERROR'
import easyscience  # now silent

docs.title: Temporary Suppression (Context Manager)
docs.text:
When you only want to silence messages during a specific operation, use the at_level context manager:

from easyscience import global_object
import logging

# Messages during the fit are suppressed, then the previous level is restored
with global_object.log.at_level(logging.ERROR):
    results = fitter.fit(x, y, weights)

This is the recommended pattern for technique-specific libraries that don't want EasyScience output to leak into their own users' consoles.

docs.title: Convenience API
docs.text:
The global_object.log object exposes a level property plus convenience methods that mirror logging module-level functions:

Member Description .level Get/set the package-root logger level ('WARNING' or logging.WARNING) .debug(msg) Log a DEBUG-level message .info(msg) Log an INFO-level message .warning(msg) Log a WARNING-level message .error(msg) Log an ERROR-level message .critical(msg) Log a CRITICAL-level message .exception(msg) Log an ERROR-level message with traceback .getLogger(name) Get a child logger under easyscience .at_level(level) Context manager for temporary level change .suspend() Suppress all EasyScience output .resume() Restore the previously set level

docs.title: Recipe 1: Keep your test output clean
docs.text:
When running tests that exercise EasyScience fitting, suppress the library's messages so they don't clutter your test reports:

import logging
from easyscience import global_object

@pytest.fixture(autouse=True)
def _quiet_easyscience():
    # The test body runs *inside* the context manager (yield within `with`)
    with global_object.log.at_level(logging.ERROR):
        yield

docs.title: Recipe 2: Library author embedding EasyScience
docs.text:
If you maintain a library that uses EasyScience internally, prevent EasyScience from writing to your users' consoles:

# In your library's __init__.py, before any EasyScience import:
import os
os.environ.setdefault('EASYSCIENCE_LOG_LEVEL', 'ERROR')

docs.title: Recipe 3: Debug mode for development
docs.text:
When developing or debugging, see all EasyScience internal diagnostics:

from easyscience import global_object

global_object.log.level = 'DEBUG'

# Your code here — all EasyScience messages will be visible

docs.title: Recipe 4: See only error messages
docs.text:
Keep the console clean but still see critical problems:

from easyscience import global_object

global_object.log.level = 'ERROR'

docs.title: Library-Safe Behaviour
docs.text:
EasyScience follows standard library-logging best practices:

  • No logging.basicConfig() — EasyScience never reconfigures the global logging setup.
  • No default stream handlers — EasyScience does not attach handlers that write to stdout or stderr. It only creates log records. Applications and test frameworks decide where those records go.
  • Child loggers inherit — Child loggers (e.g. easyscience.fitting.bumps) are left at logging.NOTSET by default, so they inherit level and handler configuration from the easyscience package-root logger. Supressing the root suppresses everything.

This means you are in full control. If you don't configure any handlers, Python's built-in logging.lastResort fallback still prints WARNING and above to stderr, so standalone users see important messages out of the box. INFO and DEBUG messages remain hidden until you opt in. If you do configure handlers (as pytest does via its logging plugin, or as an application might via basicConfig), you control what is shown and where.
